title: Die drei Feldscherer
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 118. Text from Wikisource („Die drei Feldscherer (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 118 follows three self-satisfied army surgeons who, sure they have nothing left to learn, agree at an inn to prove it by cutting off a hand, plucking out both eyes and cutting out a heart overnight, and healing themselves whole again by morning with a special salve. While the parts sit locked away, a cat gets at them and eats the heart, and the terrified maid responsible hastily substitutes a hanged thief's hand, a cat's eyes, and a pig's heart, which the three sew back on in the dark without noticing the swap. Each is left permanently altered by what he now carries — one steals without meaning to, one sees like a cat by night, one is content with pig's fare — and rather than admit to the shame of it once they work it out, the three simply extort a fat sum from the innkeeper by threatening to burn his house down, and move on, wishing all the while for their own original parts back. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, Noth, thun and müßte.

sentences.t: Drei Feldscherer reisten in der Welt, die meinten ihre Kunst ausgelernt zu haben und kamen in ein Wirthshaus, wo sie übernachten wollten.
sentences.l: Three army surgeons travelled in the world; these thought they had learnt their art out and came into an inn where they wanted to spend the night.
sentences.i: Three army surgeons were travelling about the world, believing they had nothing left to learn of their art, and they came to an inn where they meant to pass the night.
sentences.n: A Feldscherer — literally a “field-shearer” — is an army surgeon, the barber-surgeon who followed the troops and did the cutting; not a shearer of sheep. die meinten picks the three up with a demonstrative — “these thought” — not with a relative; the following und kamen shows it, since a relative clause would have sent that verb to the end. die Kunst is a craft or skill, not fine art. auslernen is to finish one’s apprenticeship, so ausgelernt haben is to have nothing left to learn — which is exactly the boast the tale is about to punish. Wirthshaus is the 1857 spelling of Wirtshaus.

sentences.t: Der Wirth fragte wo sie her wären und hinaus wollten?
sentences.l: The innkeeper asked where they were from and wanted to go out to?
sentences.i: The innkeeper asked where they came from and where they were bound.
sentences.n: wo … her and wo … hinaus split the question in two: “where from” and “where out to.” wären and wollten are the subjunctive of the reported question, and the 1857 text keeps the question mark although the question is reported, not quoted. Wirth is the 1857 spelling of Wirt.

sentences.t: „Wir ziehen auf unsere Kunst in der Welt herum.“
sentences.l: “We travel about in the world on our art.”
sentences.i: “We are travelling about the world on our craft.”
sentences.n: auf seine Kunst ziehen is the journeyman’s phrase: to travel in the exercise of one’s trade. herumziehen is separable, and its particle herum stands at the end.

sentences.t: „Zeigt mir doch einmal, was ihr könnt“ sagte der Wirth.
sentences.l: “Show me then once what you can” said the innkeeper.
sentences.i: “Just show me once what you can do,” said the innkeeper.
sentences.n: Zeigt is the plural imperative, addressed to ihr. doch einmal softens a command into “go on, just.” The 1857 text sets no comma before the speech tag.

sentences.t: Da sprach der erste er wollte seine Hand abschneiden und morgen früh wieder anheilen:
sentences.l: Then said the first he would cut his hand off and heal it on again tomorrow morning:
sentences.i: Then the first said he would cut off his hand and heal it on again in the morning:
sentences.n: wollte here is “intended to, would,” not “wanted” in the modern sense. anheilen is “to heal on(to)” — a verb made for this tale, answered below by einheilen, “to heal in.” The colon does the work of a comma between the three boasts, and the reported speech follows with no daß.

sentences.t: der zweite sprach er wollte sein Herz ausreißen und morgen früh wieder anheilen:
sentences.l: the second said he would tear his heart out and heal it on again tomorrow morning:
sentences.n: ausreißen: to tear out, separable. Each boast is built on the same frame, and the tale does not vary a word of it.

sentences.t: der dritte sprach er wollte seine Augen ausstechen und morgen früh wieder einheilen.
sentences.l: the third said he would stab his eyes out and heal them in again tomorrow morning.
sentences.i: the third said he would put out his eyes and heal them in again in the morning.
sentences.n: ausstechen is literally “to stab out,” the old phrase for putting out eyes. einheilen answers anheilen: eyes are healed back in, a hand is healed back on.

sentences.t: „Könnt ihr das,“ sprach der Wirth, „so habt ihr ausgelernt.“
sentences.l: “Can you that,” said the innkeeper, “then you have learnt out.”
sentences.i: “If you can do that,” said the innkeeper, “then you have nothing left to learn.”
sentences.n: A conditional without wenn: the verb comes first — Könnt ihr das — and so answers it, “then.” This shape is everywhere in the tales.

sentences.t: Sie hatten aber eine Salbe, was sie damit bestrichen, das heilte zusammen, und das Fläschchen, wo sie drin war, trugen sie beständig bei sich.
sentences.l: But they had a salve; whatever they smeared with it, that healed together, and the little flask where it was in they carried constantly with them.
sentences.i: But they had a salve: whatever they smeared with it healed up, and the little flask it was in they carried about with them at all times.
sentences.n: was … das … is the older correlative, “whatever …, that ….” wo sie drin war is the colloquial way of saying worin sie war, “in which it was”; drin here is plain High German, not dialect. Fläschchen is the diminutive of Flasche.

sentences.t: Da schnitten sie Hand Herz und Auge vom Leibe, wie sie gesagt hatten, legtens zusammen auf einen Teller und gabens dem Wirth:
sentences.l: Then they cut hand, heart and eye from the body, as they had said, laid them together on a plate and gave them to the innkeeper:
sentences.n: The 1857 text writes Hand Herz und Auge with no commas. legtens and gabens are legten es and gaben es run together, the es standing for the whole collection. vom Leibe: from the body, dative after von.

sentences.t: der Wirth gabs einem Mädchen, das sollts in den Schrank stellen und wohl aufheben.
sentences.l: the innkeeper gave it to a girl, that one was to set it in the cupboard and keep it well.
sentences.i: the innkeeper gave it to a girl, who was to put it in the cupboard and keep it carefully.
sentences.n: Mädchen is neuter because of the diminutive ending -chen, so the tale calls the girl das, es and sein all the way through — “it, its.” English must say “she”; the German gender is grammatical and says nothing about her. gabs is gab es, sollts is sollte es.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen aber hatte einen heimlichen Schatz, der war ein Soldat.
sentences.l: But the girl had a secret sweetheart, he was a soldier.
sentences.i: But the girl had a sweetheart in secret, and he was a soldier.
sentences.n: Schatz, “treasure,” is the everyday word for a sweetheart. der war is the demonstrative continuing the sentence where English would put a relative, “who was.”

sentences.t: Wie nun der Wirth, die drei Feldscherer und alle Leute im Haus schliefen, kam der Soldat und wollte was zu essen haben.
sentences.l: When now the innkeeper, the three army surgeons and all people in the house were sleeping, the soldier came and wanted to have something to eat.
sentences.i: Now when the innkeeper, the three army surgeons and everyone in the house were asleep, the soldier came and wanted something to eat.
sentences.n: was is the everyday short form of etwas. wie once more means “when.”

sentences.t: Da schloß das Mädchen den Schrank auf und holte ihm etwas, und über der großen Liebe vergaß es die Schrankthüre zuzumachen,
sentences.l: Then the girl unlocked the cupboard and fetched him something, and over the great love it forgot to shut the cupboard door,
sentences.i: Then the girl unlocked the cupboard and fetched him something, and in all her love she forgot to shut the cupboard door,
sentences.n: aufschließen: to unlock — separable, so auf lands at the end. über der großen Liebe: “over” in the sense of in the midst of, so taken up with. Schrankthüre keeps the 1857 th (modern Schranktür).

sentences.t: setzte sich zum Liebsten an Tisch, und sie schwätzten mit einander.
sentences.l: set herself down to her sweetheart at table, and they chatted with one another.
sentences.i: and she sat down at the table beside her sweetheart, and they chatted together.
sentences.n: sich setzen is reflexive, “to set oneself.” der Liebste is “the dearest one,” the sweetheart. schwätzen is to chat or gossip — southern colouring, not a dialect form.

sentences.t: Wie es so vergnügt saß und an kein Unglück dachte, kam die Katze hereingeschlichen, fand den Schrank offen,
sentences.l: As it sat so contentedly and thought of no misfortune, the cat came slinking in, found the cupboard open,
sentences.i: While she sat there so content and thought of no mischance, the cat came slinking in, found the cupboard open,
sentences.n: kam hereingeschlichen: German joins a verb of coming to a past participle where English uses a present participle, “came slinking in.” denken an takes the accusative.

sentences.t: nahm die Hand das Herz und die Augen der drei Feldscherer, und lief damit hinaus.
sentences.l: took the hand, the heart and the eyes of the three army surgeons, and ran out with them.
sentences.n: damit is “with that, with them” — da- plus a preposition stands in for a thing already named, and the tales use it at every turn.

sentences.t: Als nun der Soldat gegessen hatte und das Mädchen das Geräth aufheben und den Schrank zuschließen wollte,
sentences.l: When now the soldier had eaten and the girl wanted to put the gear away and lock the cupboard,
sentences.i: Now when the soldier had eaten, and the girl was about to put the things away and lock the cupboard,
sentences.n: Geräth (modern Gerät) is the gear, the dishes and utensils. aufheben here is “to put away, keep,” not “to lift”; zuschließen is to lock shut. Both infinitives hang on wollte at the end.

sentences.t: da sah es wohl daß der Teller, den ihm der Wirth aufzuheben gegeben hatte, ledig war.
sentences.l: then it saw well that the plate, which the innkeeper had given it to keep, was empty.
sentences.i: she saw plainly that the plate the innkeeper had given her to keep was empty.
sentences.n: wohl here means “plainly, well enough,” not “probably.” ledig is “empty, free of”; the modern sense “unmarried” is later. aufzuheben, an infinitive with zu, carries the purpose: given her to keep.

sentences.t: Da sagte es erschrocken zu seinem Schatz „ach, was will ich armes Mädchen anfangen!
sentences.l: Then it said frightened to its sweetheart “ah, what shall I poor girl begin!
sentences.i: Then in her fright she said to her sweetheart, “Oh, what shall I poor girl do!
sentences.n: was anfangen is the German for what to do about a thing — “what to begin.” seinem is “her,” the possessive following the neuter Mädchen. The speech runs on into the next unit, so its closing mark comes only there.

sentences.t: Die Hand ist fort, das Herz und die Augen sind auch fort, wie wird mirs morgen früh ergehen!“
sentences.l: The hand is gone, the heart and the eyes are gone too, how will it fare for me tomorrow morning!”
sentences.i: The hand is gone, the heart and the eyes are gone as well; how will it go with me in the morning!”
sentences.n: fort sein: to be gone, away. ergehen is used impersonally with a dative — mir ergeht es, “it goes for me,” our “I fare.” mirs is mir es.

sentences.t: „Sei still,“ sprach er, „ich will dir aus der Noth helfen:
sentences.l: “Be still,” said he, “I will help you out of the distress:
sentences.i: “Be still,” said he, “I will help you out of your trouble:
sentences.n: Sei is the imperative of sein. helfen takes the dative, dir. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not — need, distress, a fix.

sentences.t: es hängt ein Dieb draußen am Galgen, dem will ich die Hand abschneiden;
sentences.l: there hangs a thief outside on the gallows, from him I will cut the hand off;
sentences.i: there is a thief hanging outside on the gallows, and I will cut off his hand;
sentences.n: es hängt … is the placeholder es of existence, like our “there hangs.” dem is a dative demonstrative, “from that one,” where English says “his”: German marks the person by case and leaves die Hand a plain object. Executed criminals were left hanging on the gallows outside the town, which is why one is to hand.

sentences.t: welche Hand wars denn?“
sentences.l: which hand was it then?”
sentences.n: wars is war es. denn again is the untranslatable question-word, roughly “tell me.”

sentences.t: „Die rechte.“
sentences.l: “The right one.”
sentences.n: The girl answers with the adjective alone: German lets die rechte stand for “the right hand” without repeating the noun.

sentences.t: Da gab ihm das Mädchen ein scharfes Messer, und er gieng hin, schnitt dem armen Sünder die rechte Hand ab und brachte sie herbei.
sentences.l: Then the girl gave him a sharp knife, and he went thither, cut the poor sinner’s right hand off and brought it hither.
sentences.i: Then the girl gave him a sharp knife, and he went out, cut off the poor sinner’s right hand, and brought it back.
sentences.n: der arme Sünder is the fixed old term for a condemned criminal — “the poor sinner” — used of the man on the gallows; it is not a judgment on his soul. dem armen Sünder is the dative of the person with die Hand as the object: German says “cut the hand off to him.” hin is “thither,” herbei “hither”: the pair keeps the direction of every movement clear.

sentences.t: Darauf packte er die Katze und stach ihr die Augen aus;
sentences.l: Thereupon he seized the cat and stabbed her eyes out;
sentences.i: Thereupon he seized the cat and put out her eyes;
sentences.n: The dative of the person again, here of the animal — ihr — with die Augen as the object. ausstechen is separable, so aus stands at the end. The tale is not squeamish and it is not meant to be softened.

sentences.t: nun fehlte nur noch das Herz.
sentences.l: now was lacking only the heart.
sentences.i: now only the heart was still lacking.
sentences.n: fehlen is “to be missing,” and the thing missing is its subject. nur noch is “only … still,” the last item outstanding.

sentences.t: „Habt ihr nicht geschlachtet, und liegt das Schweinefleisch nicht im Keller?“
sentences.l: “Have you not slaughtered, and does the pork not lie in the cellar?”
sentences.i: “Have you not been slaughtering, and is the pork not lying in the cellar?”
sentences.n: schlachten, to slaughter a beast, was done at a set season, so the question is really “is it not your killing-time?” Schweinefleisch is “swine-flesh,” pork.

sentences.t: „Ja“ sagte das Mädchen.
sentences.l: “Yes” said the girl.
sentences.n: Again no comma before the speech tag, as the 1857 text prints it.

sentences.t: „Nun, das ist gut“ sagte der Soldat, gieng hinunter und holte ein Schweineherz.
sentences.l: “Now, that is good” said the soldier, went down and fetched a pig’s heart.
sentences.i: “Well, that is good,” said the soldier, and he went down and fetched a pig’s heart.
sentences.n: Nun as an opener is “well.” The German runs the speech tag and the next two verbs on one subject, so English has to supply “and he.”

sentences.t: Das Mädchen that alles zusammen auf den Teller, und stellte ihn in den Schrank, und als ihr Liebster darauf Abschied genommen hatte, legte es sich ruhig ins Bett.
sentences.l: The girl put everything together on the plate, and set it in the cupboard, and when her sweetheart thereupon had taken leave, it laid itself calmly in bed.
sentences.i: The girl put everything together on the plate and set it in the cupboard, and when her sweetheart had taken his leave, she went calmly to bed.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat (thun for tun). Abschied nehmen: to take one’s leave. Here the tale writes ihr Liebster with the feminine possessive and then returns to the neuter es — the two genders stand side by side in one sentence.

sentences.t: Morgens, als die Feldscherer aufstanden, sagten sie dem Mädchen es sollte ihnen den Teller holen, darauf Hand Herz und Augen lägen.
sentences.l: In the morning, when the army surgeons got up, they told the girl it should fetch them the plate, on which hand, heart and eyes lay.
sentences.i: In the morning, when the army surgeons rose, they told the girl to fetch them the plate on which hand, heart and eyes were lying.
sentences.n: Morgens is the genitive of time, “of a morning.” darauf, “thereon,” is the older way of saying worauf, “on which.” lägen is subjunctive: the parts lie there in the surgeons’ account of the matter, and the tale is careful to mark whose account it is.

sentences.t: Da brachte es ihn aus dem Schrank, und der erste hielt sich die Diebshand an und bestrich sie mit seiner Salbe, alsbald war sie ihm angewachsen.
sentences.l: Then it brought it out of the cupboard, and the first held the thief’s hand on himself and smeared it with his salve, at once it had grown on to him.
sentences.i: Then she brought it out of the cupboard, and the first held the thief’s hand to himself and smeared it with his salve, and at once it had grown fast to him.
sentences.n: sich anhalten: to hold something on oneself, the dative sich showing whose arm it is. anwachsen, “to grow on,” takes sein in the past — war … angewachsen. Diebshand is a compound the tale coins on the spot.

sentences.t: Der zweite nahm die Katzenaugen und heilte sie ein:
sentences.l: The second took the cat’s eyes and healed them in:
sentences.n: einheilen again, the made verb of this tale; the particle ein closes the clause.

sentences.t: der dritte machte das Schweineherz fest.
sentences.l: the third made the pig’s heart fast.
sentences.i: the third fixed the pig’s heart in place.
sentences.n: festmachen: to make fast, fasten — separable, so fest comes last. Three sentences, three men, three grafts, and no wonder is made of any of it.

sentences.t: Der Wirth aber stand dabei, bewunderte ihre Kunst und sagte dergleichen hätt er noch nicht gesehen, er wollte sie bei jedermann rühmen und empfehlen.
sentences.l: But the innkeeper stood by, admired their art and said the like he had not yet seen, he would praise and recommend them to everybody.
sentences.i: But the innkeeper stood by, admired their art, and said he had never seen the like; he would praise and recommend them to everyone.
sentences.n: dergleichen: “the like, such a thing.” hätt … gesehen and wollte are the subjunctive of reported speech. bei jedermann: “with everybody,” that is, to everyone he met.

sentences.t: Darauf bezahlten sie ihre Zeche und reisten weiter.
sentences.l: Thereupon they paid their reckoning and travelled on.
sentences.n: die Zeche is the bill at an inn. weiterreisen is separable, weiter at the end.

sentences.t: Wie sie so dahin giengen, so blieb der mit dem Schweineherzen gar nicht bei ihnen, sondern wo eine Ecke war, lief er hin und schnüffelte darin herum, wie Schweine thun.
sentences.l: As they were going along so, the one with the pig’s heart did not stay with them at all, but where a corner was, he ran thither and snuffled about in it, as swine do.
sentences.i: As they went along, the one with the pig’s heart would not keep with them at all; wherever there was a corner he ran to it and snuffled about in it, as swine do.
sentences.n: der mit dem Schweineherzen: German makes a whole person out of “the one with ….” The doubled so — Wie sie so dahin giengen, so blieb — picks the when-clause up again, and English drops the second one. thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Die andern wollten ihn an dem Rockschlippen zurückhalten, aber das half nichts, er riß sich los und lief hin, wo der dickste Unrath lag.
sentences.l: The others wanted to hold him back by the coat-tail, but that helped nothing, he tore himself loose and ran thither where the thickest filth lay.
sentences.i: The others tried to hold him back by his coat-tails, but it was no use; he tore himself loose and ran to where the filth lay thickest.
sentences.n: wollten here is “tried to.” German takes hold of a person by a garment with an — an dem Rockschlippen. Unrath (modern Unrat) is filth, refuse, muck.

sentences.t: Der zweite stellte sich auch wunderlich an, rieb die Augen und sagte zu dem andern „Kamerad, was ist das?
sentences.l: The second behaved himself strangely too, rubbed his eyes and said to the other “comrade, what is that?
sentences.i: The second behaved strangely as well: he rubbed his eyes and said to the other, “Comrade, what is this?
sentences.n: sich anstellen: to behave, to carry on — reflexive, with the particle an at the end. wunderlich is “odd, queer,” never “wonderful.”

sentences.t: das sind meine Augen nicht, ich sehe ja nichts, leite mich doch einer, daß ich nicht falle.“
sentences.l: these are my eyes not, I see nothing indeed, let one of you lead me, that I do not fall.”
sentences.i: these are not my eyes, I see nothing at all; let one of you lead me, so that I do not fall.”
sentences.n: leite … einer is an imperative with a subject attached — “let someone lead me,” einer standing for “one of you.” ja inside a sentence is not “yes” but an emphasis, “you see, indeed.” daß gives the purpose: so that I do not fall.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie mit Mühe fort bis zum Abend, wo sie zu einer andern Herberge kamen.
sentences.l: Then they went on with difficulty until evening, where they came to another lodging.
sentences.i: So they went on with trouble until evening, when they came to another inn.
sentences.n: mit Mühe: with effort, with difficulty. wo here is temporal, “when” — German allows it after a word of time.

sentences.t: Sie traten zusammen in die Wirthsstube, da saß in einer Ecke ein reicher Herr vorm Tisch und zählte Geld.
sentences.l: They stepped together into the taproom, there sat in a corner a rich gentleman before the table and counted money.
sentences.i: They stepped together into the taproom, and there in a corner sat a rich gentleman at the table counting money.
sentences.n: die Wirthsstube is the public room of an inn. vorm is vor dem run together. German strings the two verbs saß … und zählte where English prefers a participle, “sat counting.”

sentences.t: Der mit der Diebshand gieng um ihn herum, zuckte ein paarmal mit dem Arm,
sentences.l: The one with the thief’s hand went around him, twitched a couple of times with the arm,
sentences.i: The one with the thief’s hand walked round him and twitched his arm a few times,
sentences.n: um … herum, “around about,” is a two-part frame with the object inside it. zucken mit puts the limb in the dative as the thing twitched with.

sentences.t: endlich, wie der Herr sich umwendete, griff er in den Haufen hinein und nahm eine Hand voll Geld heraus.
sentences.l: at last, as the gentleman turned himself round, he reached into the heap in and took a hand full of money out.
sentences.i: at last, when the gentleman turned round, he reached into the heap and took out a handful of money.
sentences.n: sich umwenden: to turn oneself round, reflexive and separable. hineingreifen and herausnehmen each keep their particle at the end — one motion in, one out. eine Hand voll is printed as three words in 1857.

sentences.t: Der eine sahs und sprach „Kamerad, was machst du?
sentences.l: The one saw it and said “comrade, what are you doing?
sentences.i: One of them saw it and said, “Comrade, what are you about?
sentences.n: sahs is sah es. der eine, “the one,” means one of the other two.

sentences.t: stehlen darfst du nicht, schäm dich!“
sentences.l: steal you may not, shame yourself!”
sentences.i: you must not steal — for shame!”
sentences.n: The infinitive stehlen is thrown to the front for emphasis, which puts darfst in second place and the subject after it. sich schämen is reflexive: “shame yourself” is the German for “be ashamed.”

sentences.t: „Ei,“ sagte er, „was kann ich dafür!
sentences.l: “Eh,” said he, “what can I for it!
sentences.i: “Why,” said he, “how am I to blame for it!
sentences.n: was kann ich dafür is a fixed phrase with its verb left out — “what can I [do] for it,” meaning “it is not my fault.” The literal leaves the gap open rather than filling it.

sentences.t: es zuckt mir in der Hand, ich muß zugreifen, ich mag wollen oder nicht.“
sentences.l: it twitches me in the hand, I must grasp to, I may want to or not.”
sentences.i: it twitches in my hand, I have to snatch, whether I will or not.”
sentences.n: mir is the dative of the person: “it twitches to me in the hand,” where English says “in my hand.” zugreifen: to grab, to help oneself. ich mag wollen oder nicht is “I may will or not,” our “whether I want to or not.”

sentences.t: Sie legten sich danach schlafen, und wie sie da liegen, ists so finster, daß man keine Hand vor Augen sehen kann.
sentences.l: They laid themselves down to sleep after that, and as they lie there, it is so dark that one can see no hand before one’s eyes.
sentences.i: After that they lay down to sleep, and as they lie there it is so dark that you cannot see a hand before your eyes.
sentences.n: sich schlafen legen: to lay oneself down to sleep. The tale slips out of the past into the present — liegen, ists — as spoken storytelling does, and the literal keeps the shift. ists is ist es.

sentences.t: Auf einmal erwachte der mit den Katzenaugen, weckte die andern und sprach „Brüder, schaut einmal auf, seht ihr die weißen Mäuschen, die da herumlaufen?“
sentences.l: All at once the one with the cat’s eyes awoke, woke the others and said “brothers, look up once, do you see the little white mice that run about there?”
sentences.i: All at once the one with the cat’s eyes woke, woke the others, and said, “Brothers, look up: do you see the little white mice running about there?”
sentences.n: aufschauen: to look up — separable, so schaut … auf with einmal (“just once”) between. Mäuschen, the diminutive of Maus, is neuter. The joke is that the mice are really there: cats’ eyes see in the dark, and his companions cannot.

sentences.t: Die zwei richteten sich auf, konnten aber nichts sehen.
sentences.l: The two raised themselves up, but could see nothing.
sentences.i: The other two sat up, but could see nothing.
sentences.n: sich aufrichten: to raise oneself, to sit up — reflexive and separable.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „es ist mit uns nicht richtig, wir haben das Unsrige nicht wieder gekriegt, wir müssen zurück nach dem Wirth, der hat uns betrogen.“
sentences.l: Then he said “it is not right with us, we have not got the ours again, we must back to the innkeeper, he has cheated us.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “There is something wrong with us; we have not got our own back again; we must go back to the innkeeper — he has cheated us.”
sentences.n: es ist nicht richtig mit uns: something is not right with us. das Unsrige is “what is ours, our own.” wir müssen zurück has no verb of motion at all: müssen carries it alone. kriegen is the everyday word for “get.”

sentences.t: Also machten sie sich am andern Morgen dahin auf und sagten dem Wirth sie hätten ihr richtig Werk nicht wieder gekriegt,
sentences.l: So they set themselves off thither the next morning and told the innkeeper they had not got their right work back again,
sentences.i: So the next morning they set off there and told the innkeeper that they had not got their proper parts back,
sentences.n: sich aufmachen: to set out — reflexive, with auf at the end. am andern Morgen: “on the other morning,” the next one. richtig Werk is uninflected, the older form of richtiges Werk — “the proper article, what is rightly theirs.”

sentences.t: der eine hätte eine Diebshand, der zweite Katzenaugen, und der dritte ein Schweineherz.
sentences.l: the one had a thief’s hand, the second cat’s eyes, and the third a pig’s heart.
sentences.i: one of them had a thief’s hand, the second cat’s eyes, and the third a pig’s heart.
sentences.n: hätte is subjunctive: this is still their report to the innkeeper, not the narrator speaking. The verb is not repeated in the second and third clauses.

sentences.t: Der Wirth sprach daran müßte das Mädchen Schuld sein und wollte es rufen,
sentences.l: The innkeeper said thereon must the girl be to blame and wanted to call it,
sentences.i: The innkeeper said the girl must be to blame for it, and was going to call her,
sentences.n: an etwas Schuld sein: to be to blame for something, with daran pointing back at the whole business. müßte is the subjunctive of reported speech (1857 spelling of müsste).

sentences.t: aber wie das die drei hatte kommen sehen, war es zum Hinterpförtchen fortgelaufen, und kam nicht wieder.
sentences.l: but when it had seen the three coming, it had run off out at the little back gate, and did not come again.
sentences.i: but when she had seen the three coming, she had run off out of the little back gate, and did not come back.
sentences.n: hatte kommen sehen is the double infinitive: after another infinitive, sehen keeps its infinitive form instead of becoming gesehen. das and es are the girl again. Hinterpförtchen is the diminutive of Hinterpforte, the little back gate — she goes out the way servants went.

sentences.t: Da sprachen die drei er sollte ihnen viel Geld geben, sonst ließen sie ihm den rothen Hahn übers Haus fliegen:
sentences.l: Then the three said he should give them much money, otherwise they would let the red cock fly over his house:
sentences.i: Then the three said he must give them a great deal of money, or they would set the red cock flying over his house:
sentences.n: den rothen Hahn übers Haus fliegen lassen is the old phrase for setting a house alight — the red cock is the flame running along the roof. It is a threat of arson and the innkeeper understands it at once. rothen is the 1857 spelling of roten.

sentences.t: da gab er was er hatte und nur aufbringen konnte, und die drei zogen damit fort.
sentences.l: then he gave what he had and could possibly raise, and the three moved off with it.
sentences.i: then he gave what he had and all he could raise, and the three went off with it.
sentences.n: nur here means “at all, possibly” — was er nur aufbringen konnte: whatever he could possibly scrape together. aufbringen: to raise, to produce money.

sentences.t: Es war für ihr Lebtag genug, sie hätten aber doch lieber ihr richtig Werk gehabt.
sentences.l: It was enough for their life-day, but they would rather have had their right work.
sentences.i: It was enough for their lifetime, but they would rather have had their own proper parts back.
sentences.n: für ihr Lebtag is an old fixed phrase, “for their life-day,” for as long as they live. hätten … gehabt with lieber is the subjunctive of the wish: they would sooner have had. The tale ends on what was lost, not on the money — and the three quacks are never punished for the boast that began it.

glossary.aufheben: aufheben — to keep, put away safely (separable, particle auf; elsewhere also: to lift up)
glossary.aufzuheben: aufheben — to keep, put away safely (zu-infinitive; separable, particle auf)
glossary.ausreißen: ausreißen — to tear out (separable, particle aus; elsewhere also: to bolt, run away)
glossary.drin: drin — in it, inside (colloquial High German, short for darin)
glossary.ergehen: ergehen — to fare, to go with someone (impersonal, with the dative: wie ergeht es ihm, how does it go with him)
glossary.ledig: ledig — empty, bare (adj.; also: free of, rid of)
glossary.rechte: recht — right, right-hand (inflected; die rechte Hand)
glossary.richtig: richtig — right, proper (uninflected before a noun in richtig Werk; also: in order, as it should be)
glossary.schatz: der Schatz — treasure; also the everyday word for a sweetheart, darling
glossary.stach: stechen — stabbed, put out (3rd sg. past; ausstechen: stach ihm die Augen aus)
glossary.stellen: stellen — to put, set (something upright); sich stellen: to place oneself
glossary.sünder: der Sünder — sinner; der arme Sünder is the fixed term for a criminal under sentence of death
glossary.werk: das Werk — work, piece of work (ihr richtig Werk: what is rightly theirs, their own proper article)
glossary.zogen: ziehen — went, journeyed on (3rd pl. past; separable weiterziehen/fortziehen — not “pulled” here)
